## Overview

The Maidu are a Native American people of northern California who reside in the central Sierra Nevada, especially in the watershed areas of the Feather and American Rivers and in Humbug Valley. Their local divisions include the Nisenan or Southern Maidu, the Northeastern or Mountain Maidu, also known as Yamani Maidu, and the Konkow, or Koyom'kawi/Concow. The Mechoopda live in the area of Chico, California. Estimates of the pre-contact population vary: Alfred L. Kroeber estimated 9,000 people in 1770, while Sherburne F. Cook estimated 9,500; the 1930 census counted 93, and the population was estimated at 3,500 in 1995. In Maiduan languages, *maidu* means “person.” Maidu languages have been associated by some linguists with the Penutian language group, although that classification is disputed.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Basketry** — Maidu women were skilled basketweavers who used both coiled and twining techniques. They made baskets ranging from thimbles to 10 or more feet in diameter, as well as large storage baskets, bowls, shallow trays, traps, cradles, hats, and seed beaters.

**Plant-fiber weaving** — Weaving materials included wild plant stems, barks, roots, and leaves. Fern roots, red bark of the redbud, white willow twigs, tule roots, hazel twigs, yucca leaves, brown marsh grassroots, and sedge roots were among the materials used.

**Geometric basket designs** — Combining plant materials produced red, black, white, brown, or tan geometric designs. Baskets could also be decorated with feathers of brightly plumaged birds, shells, quills, seeds, or beads.

**Acorn granary weaving** — Maidu weavers created above-ground acorn granaries for storing large quantities of acorns for harder times.

**Seed beaters** — Seed beaters were among the objects made through basketry and weaving practices, alongside traps, cradles, hats, bowls, and trays.

**Decorated coiled and twined products** — Maidu basketry products were sometimes handsomely decorated according to the inventiveness and skill of the weaver and the materials available.

**Storage baskets** — Large storage baskets formed part of the material system used to preserve gathered foods, especially the substantial quantities of acorns collected and processed by the Maidu.

**Motif vocabulary.** Red, black, white, brown, and tan geometric designs; no named individual motifs are given in the sources.

### Clothing & dress

 They do record hats among the objects made by Maidu basketweavers. The sources also mention feathers, shells, quills, seeds, and beads as materials that could be attached to woven products. The Kuksu or “big head” dances are described as part of the religious tradition.

### Architecture

Maidu dwellings in the hills and mountains were partially underground, providing protection from the cold. These houses were circular structures 12 to 18 feet in diameter, with floors dug as much as 3 feet below ground level. A pole framework was built over the excavated floor and covered with pinebark slabs; a sturdy layer of earth was placed along the base. The central fire stood at ground level in a stone-lined pit, with bedrock mortar used to hold heat for food preparation.

For summer use, the Maidu built a different kind of shelter from cut branches tied together and fastened to sapling posts. These shelters were covered with brush and soil. Their principal opening faced east, both to catch the rising sun and to avoid the heat of the afternoon sun.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They do document wooden, stone, and woven objects associated with food preparation and household life. These include pestles, hollowed-out stones, stone-lined fire pits, bedrock mortars, large storage baskets, bowls, shallow trays, traps, cradles, hats, and seed beaters. Acorns were shelled, cleaned, and ground into meal by pounding them with a pestle on a hard surface, generally a hollowed-out stone.

### Jewelry & body adornment

 Feathers of brightly plumaged birds, shells, quills, seeds, and beads are identified as materials that could be attached to woven products.

## Music & performance

The principal named performance tradition in the sources is the Kuksu cult, a central California religious system based on a male secret society. It was characterized by Kuksu or “big head” dances. Maidu leaders were typically selected from men who headed the local Kuksu cult. These leaders were primarily responsible for settling internal disputes and negotiating matters between villages, rather than exercising day-to-day authority. The Kuksu cult system was also followed by the Pomo and the Patwin among the Wintun. Missionaries later forced the peoples to adopt Christianity, although elements of traditional practices were often retained.

## Dance & theatre

The Maidu religious tradition included the Kuksu or “big head” dances, associated with the Kuksu cult and its male secret society.

A traditional spring celebration was the Bear Dance. During this celebration, the Maidu honored the bear coming out of hibernation. The bear’s hibernation and survival through the winter symbolized perseverance, and the Maidu identified with the animal spiritually.

## Festivals & rituals

The Bear Dance was a traditional spring celebration during which the Maidu honored the bear coming out of hibernation. The bear’s survival through winter symbolized perseverance, and the animal held spiritual significance for the Maidu.

Maidu elder Marie Mason Potts described a daily religious pattern in which the Maidu greeted the sunrise with a prayer of thankfulness, stopped at noon for meditation, and at sunset communed with Kadyapam and gave thanks for blessings throughout the day. The Kuksu cult was a central religious institution and included the Kuksu or “big head” dances.

## Foodways

Acorns were the Maidu’s principal dietary staple after being processed and prepared. The Maidu tended local groves of oak trees to maximize acorn production. Preparing acorns was a long process undertaken by women and children: the acorns were shelled, cleaned, and ground into meal by pounding them with a pestle on a hard surface, generally a hollowed-out stone.

The tannic acid was leached from the meal by spreading it over a bed of pine needles laid over sand. Cedar or fir boughs were placed across the meal, and warm water was poured over it. The boughs distributed the water evenly and flavored the meal. The Maidu stored large quantities of acorns in above-ground granaries created by weavers.

Other foods included edible roots and tubers, seeds from flowering plants, corms from wildflowers, deer, elk, antelope, smaller game, and fish. Salmon were collected when they came upstream to spawn, while other fish were available year-round. The Maidu also ate grasshoppers and crickets, roots, stems, leaves, sugar pine nuts, and yellow pine nuts. Nuts could be eaten raw or cooked into soup. Manzanita berries were crushed and mixed with water to make a thick dough; when more water was added, the mixture produced a drink known as *manzanita cider*. Wild mint was brewed as tea.

## Oral tradition & literature

Maidu traditional narratives prominently feature K'odojapem, the World-maker, and Wepam, Trickster Coyote. The Maidu language source gives *wepa* as the word for “coyote” and includes Coyote in grammatical examples, including expressions referring to Coyote’s flour. Language revitalization efforts have been active since 2004. As of 2011, classes in Maidu were available in Nevada County, California. Farrell Cunningham taught Mountain Maidu language classes in Greenville, Susanville, Nevada City, and Auburn and was active with the Maidu Theater in Nevada City until his death on August 11, 2013, at age 37.

## Language & religion

Maidu, also called Northeastern Maidu or Mountain Maidu, is an extinct Maiduan language of California, United States. Related languages include Konkow and Nisenan, along with the Chico language and other extinct variations. The four principal divisions named in the sources are Northeastern Maidu or Yamonee Maidu, Southern Maidu or Nisenan, Northwestern Maidu or Konkow, and Valley Maidu or Chico.

Some linguists associate the Maiduan language family with the Penutian language group, alongside Miwok, Wintun, Yokuts, and Ohlone, but this classification is disputed. Maidu distinguishes singular, dual, and plural, and its nouns receive one of ten possible case markings. The primary religious tradition was the Kuksu cult. Maidu elder Marie Mason Potts described the Maidu as traditionally monotheistic. Missionaries later forced the peoples to adopt Christianity, while elements of traditional practice were often retained.
